title: Band Theory
description: Ten original questions on atomic energy levels, interactions between atoms, band formation, band occupancy and the electrical behaviour of solids. Multiple-response items use +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero. Includes spin-state counting, direct/indirect transitions and optical attenuation.

questions.prompt: Which ideas belong to the simplified Bohr model of an isolated atom?

options.content: A transition between allowed levels exchanges a photon whose energy matches the level difference.
An electron bound to the atom may have any continuous energy.
The model predicts that every allowed orbit immediately collapses into the nucleus.
Electrons occupy allowed orbits with discrete energies.

questions.explanation: The Bohr model postulates stationary allowed states with quantized energies. Absorption or emission accompanies a transition and satisfies $\Delta E=hf$. The model deliberately avoids the classical prediction of continuous radiation and orbital collapse.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 4-8

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy one spatial atomic orbital?

options.content: Two, with opposite spin states
One
Four
Any number if their kinetic energies differ

questions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most two electrons in one spatial orbital, and they must have opposite spins. This occupancy rule becomes important when many atomic states split into bands.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 9-15

questions.prompt: When two identical atoms are brought close enough for their electron wavefunctions to overlap, what can occur?

options.content: Bonding and antibonding combinations can form.
The levels necessarily become farther apart as the atoms are separated to infinity.
Interaction halves the total number of spatial states.
A formerly degenerate atomic level can split into two distinct levels.
Every split spatial orbital can hold only one electron, regardless of spin.
The splitting generally grows as the interaction becomes stronger.

questions.explanation: Overlap couples the originally identical states and lifts their degeneracy, producing lower-energy bonding and higher-energy antibonding combinations. Stronger interaction normally produces greater separation; it does not remove all allowed states. Each spatial orbital can hold two electrons of opposite spins. Interaction changes energies and wavefunctions, not the dimension of the orbital basis. At infinite separation the interaction-induced splitting vanishes.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 17-21

questions.prompt: The diagram shows band formation. Consider one spatial atomic orbital per atom, for N identical atoms. Ignore spin-dependent splitting. Which statements are correct?

image.alt: Atomic energy levels splitting into dense upper and lower allowed energy bands separated by a forbidden gap.

options.content: Every energy becomes allowed, so forbidden gaps cannot exist.
Each atomic level produces many closely spaced allowed levels that appear as a band.
A range with no allowed states may remain between bands.
The resulting band contains N spatial states and can accommodate 2N electrons including spin.

questions.explanation: The N spatial orbitals combine into N spatial states (energy levels may remain degenerate). Each spatial state supports two spin states, so the band can accommodate 2N electrons. A macroscopic solid has densely spaced levels, but forbidden energy intervals can remain between bands.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 18 and 22-24

questions.prompt: A completely filled energy band normally produces no net electrical current under a small applied field because contributions from occupied states cancel.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: In a full band, every state with one velocity has a corresponding occupied state with the opposite velocity. A small field cannot simply move electrons into already occupied nearby states, so the full band has no net current contribution.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slide 28

questions.prompt: Which band arrangements can give metallic electrical behaviour?

options.content: A filled band overlaps an empty band in energy.
A full valence band is separated from an empty conduction band by a very large gap.
All nearby states are forbidden at the electron energy.
The highest occupied band is only partly filled.

questions.explanation: A partly filled band contains nearby empty states into which electrons can move, and overlapping bands also provide accessible states. A full band separated by a large gap lacks such states and is associated with insulating behaviour.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 28-30

questions.prompt: For an intrinsic semiconductor, which qualitative effects are expected when temperature rises?

options.content: Excitation leaves mobile vacancies, or holes, in the valence band.
Holes carry the same effective charge sign as conduction electrons.
Thermal promotion creates a conduction electron without leaving any valence-band vacancy.
More electrons can be thermally excited across the band gap.
The number of available charge carriers generally increases.

questions.explanation: Thermal energy promotes some valence electrons into the conduction band. Each excitation creates a conduction electron and a valence-band hole, increasing the carrier population. Temperature does not make the gap infinite. Holes have positive effective charge. Each intrinsic excitation creates an electron and a hole.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 31-33

questions.prompt: A slab has absorption coefficient $\alpha=2.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ at a chosen photon energy. Ignore reflection. What fraction of incident intensity remains after a thickness of $0.50\ \mu\mathrm{m}$?

options.content: Approximately 0.632
Exactly 0.500

questions.explanation: Convert the thickness to $5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Beer-Lambert attenuation gives $I/I_0=e^{-\alpha x}=e^{-1}$. The fraction absorbed is $1-e^{-1}\approx0.632$, not the fraction transmitted; a factor-of-ten unit error produces $e^{-10}$.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slide 42; EE3431C Crystal and band theory tutorial.pdf, page 3, Q7

questions.prompt: For an ideal intrinsic semiconductor at T = 0 K, which statements about the band model are correct?

options.content: The conduction band is the next higher allowed band into which electrons can be excited.
The full valence band is the highest occupied band.
The valence and conduction bands are two names for the same fully occupied band.
The band gap between them contains no allowed electron states in the ideal crystal model.

questions.explanation: At 0 K, the ideal intrinsic semiconductor has a full valence band and an empty conduction band. The valence band is therefore the highest occupied band. The ideal forbidden gap contains no allowed electronic states; finite-temperature excitation or impurity states require additional qualifications.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 26 and 31

questions.prompt: In an E-k band diagram, material P has its conduction-band minimum directly above its valence-band maximum at the same k. Material Q has these extrema at different k. Which statements are correct?

options.content: A band-edge transition in Q generally needs a phonon to help conserve crystal momentum.
Q cannot absorb light at any photon energy.
A direct band gap must have zero energy.
P has a direct band gap.
A photon alone readily supplies any required change across the Brillouin zone.

questions.explanation: P is direct because its band-edge extrema have the same k. Photon momentum is small on the crystal-momentum scale, so an indirect band-edge transition in Q needs phonon assistance. Direct does not mean zero gap, and indirect does not forbid all optical absorption.
questions.source: EE3431C Band Theory with gif 2.pdf, slides 38-41
